Ingredients:

1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie

Directions:

1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

Anyway, this is a great game...until it's not. And in the true ending, there was a LOT of annoying, loud audio, so brace your ears for it. Imscared is one of those games that you just have to play yourself. This game is filled with horror elements and unsettling atmospheres, so if you like that stuff, you would enjoy this game. This game does contain sensitive themes, so keep that in mind.

A cute little meta-horror experience well worth its extremely cheap asking price.

Only a few complaints which weren't enough to ruin the overall experience for me, but your mileage may vary:

- The game can sometimes be a pain to get running properly depending on your system setup. It needs to be able to create a folder on your desktop and place files in there, among other things. In my instance I had to fight with my PC's security and antivirus software for quite a while before I could convince them that the game was harmless.

- The game likes to close itself [i]a lot[/i]. Collected a key item? Closed. Caught by the monster? Closed. Looked at something the wrong way? Closed. Oftentimes closing and restarting the game is required in order to progress or even move between locations. You sometimes have to do this multiple times in the span of just a couple minutes. It can get very tedious.

- There are an unfortunate amount of jumpscares which is a shame considering the atmosphere and environments are otherwise quite good with lots of neat set pieces.

If any of the above doesn't sound like a dealbreaker to you then jump right in and have fun. It's worth a romp. Just mind your ears with all the screaming it'll be doing at you later on.

IMSCARED was a great experience. Here's my spoiler-free review.

[hr]
You might have heard this game act like a virus: it definetely breaks the fourth wall, and I think it's one of the games that do it best.
It's full of puzzles that require you to think outside the box, in a lot of different ways.

[hr]
The atmosphere is so well made, it really gives you chill, not through stupid and random jumpscares, but by creating an environment so unique, with its own artstyle and sound design you won't encounter anywhere else.

[hr]
The story is... something. It's fascinating, probably a bit complicated to understand, but isn't that beautiful?
Discovering it bit by bit while playing was awesome.

[hr]
The playtime might not be very long, but, in the roughly 4 hours I've played, I've seen so many things that it feels like I've been playing for way longer, considering it took me a month to finish the whole game, as I split the gameplay in various sessions (and sometimes got stuck on a puzzle).
The game costs so little, I think it's totally worth it. Really reccomended!

Honestly one of the best horror games I've ever played. I even had to shut the game off and take a break for a while when I first tried playing the game and saw the entity for the first time, only for it to slowly hover backwards into the darkness. I was only a few minutes in.

The does make occasional use of jumpscares, but more often than that it uses suspense and terror to scare you. The feeling of knowing the entity is in the room with you but not knowing where it is; running away from the entity as it moves just a little bit faster than you do; having a terrifying, high-pitched, zombie-like groaning in your ears as the entity gets closer and closer.

[h2]I'm not usually into first person horror games, but I've got an immense amount of respect for this one[/h2]

I thoroughly enjoyed this, I hope I'm not over-hyping the scare factor of this game by saying I was on the brink of a heart attack, I don't usually play horror games, if I do they're typically RPG maker horror games which aren't quite as immersive, but still provide that horror atmosphere, I think the main reason I gravitate to that style of horror is it feels like it takes more to get the player scared, you have to really craft the atmosphere, earn the scares, or it'll fall flat, but I really enjoyed this game's style of horror

My main issue with first person horror games is the over-reliance on jump scares that many developers can use as a crutch, it makes the scares not feel earned, it makes the rest of the game feel less polished overall, etcetera, I won't pretend this game doesn't have jumpscares, but I felt they all worked, they weren't overdone, they were to some extent earned, or they served a purpose, you'd think it'd be easy to go "you got caught, jumpscare, go back and try again", but here it just closes, this game recognises something many horror games don't, the suspense is infinitely scarier than any jumpscare could be

For the majority of the game I was holding my breath, genuinely, I had to take breaks to just focus on breathing, that suspense, that "what could happen?" Is so much scarier than anything actually happening ever could be, and this game utilises that fact masterfully, it's not a dime a dozen horror game where everything is just repainted slightly and you're asked to shill out £20 for your reskinned slop

It has it's issues, that tag segment towards the start I'm sure some people would get confused and not know what the game wanted them to do, but at the very least, the game tells you from the start "hey, this game messes with you, you might get stuck but try to think outside the box", very few of the puzzles did I require a guide for because I had been given an idea of what to expect, and it's important to know when to let your player know what to expect, it can ruin a game, it can enhance a game, it's a case by case thing

If you like horror that earns it's scare factor, which treats you with a level of respect instead of going "it's scary, they'll slurp it up no matter what", absolutely give this a go, even if you're not a horror fan, if you think you can make it through this I think you should try, don't underestimate it though, because I did, before you open the game for that first time be mentally prepared

I realise I've been hyping this up quite a lot, and I'm sure a lot of that comes from the fact I don't really do this style of horror games very often, this was a bit of an exception because of my love of yume nikki and this game's obvious inspiration, but I do have to admit, at a point you stop being scared;

Much like another fourth wall breaking game, oneshot, you may start to figure things out and breeze through it, but for your first experience of each area I think it's still just perfectly terrifying, the atmosphere, the scares, the designs, the music, even just the way everything is laid out is perfect to make you feel uneasy, although you can also start to get a feel for when you're safe and when you're not, which is a bit of a double edged sword, I'm sure some players will pick up on that quickly and the atmosphere and fear will dissipate quickly for them, but I feel that even with that this game's horror holds up for most people


At the end of the day, it's £2.79, even if I am overhyping it, it's hardly a big ask, and it's an iconic piece of horror game history, anyone who considers themselves a horror aficionado should play this game at least once to completion

I recently played the game "Imscared" and I have to say, it was a unique and unsettling experience. The game is described as a "metaphysical horror game," and it definitely lived up to that description.

The game starts off innocently enough, with the player exploring a seemingly abandoned house. However, as you progress through the game, things start to get more and more surreal and disturbing. The atmosphere of the game is incredibly effective at creating a sense of unease and fear.

One of the things that really sets "Imscared" apart from other horror games is its use of meta elements. The game actively breaks the fourth wall and plays with the player's expectations and perceptions in clever ways. It's hard to go into too much detail without spoiling the game, but suffice it to say that "Imscared" takes some unexpected turns that left me feeling deeply disturbed and uncomfortable.

Overall, "Imscared" is a unique and highly effective horror game that I would recommend to fans of the genre. Just be prepared for a truly unsettling experience.

This game is best played going in blind, but you may have to look up a walkthrough at some point; the developer watched me stream my 6th replay of IMSCARED on Twitch once, and we [b] both [/b] forgot what to do at a certain point in the game.

There's an episode of Star Trek the Next Generation where Commander Riker pretends to be Sherlock Holmes in the Holodeck. However, he makes a critical mistake when he asks the Holodeck for a puzzle that would prove difficult for "Riker", and not "Holmes". This enables the Holodeck to create an experience that starts to mess with his mind by convincing him he is in other areas of the ship. This is similar to the experience of Imscared. The game has elements outside of just running the application that are necessary for the story to progress, and a player has to keep an open mind to succeed.
A pleasant surprise from this game is it manages to be scary while giving your character a reasonable movement speed, and avoiding artificial game lengtheners. The experience is short only because it respects your time. This game absolutely nails getting to the fun, scary, exploration constantly.
There are parts of the game that I definitely had to reference a walk through to understand, but I also lack patience and that's how I experience most horror games.
The game contains a variety of jump scares, but I wouldn't describe them as cheap shots. Some have complained about the volume of them, but I would just suggest playing without headphones.

TLDR:

I'm going to try to keep the review as spoiler-free as I possibly can, because it's a game that the less you know about it, the better, but tldr; I would say IMSCARED is the best horror game I've played, but it's more like an incredibly unique experience that no other horror game I've seen has done, and is the FIRST horror game I would recommend to anyone interested in horror, outside of even just horror games as a whole. 

Most, if not all games I play that I thoroughly loved and enjoyed, tend to stick in the back of my mind for a week or two, and that's probably how it is for most people on here, too. And although I didn't spend many hours playing IMSCARED, as I do with most other games I love that live in my head rent-free for weeks, the limited time I had for it felt a lot longer than the number steam says I have in the game! 

Despite its age (2016 is the remaster afaik) the pixel style/art hasn't aged bad (In fact I LOVE it! Popular pixel horror is rare nowadays), moreso it retains the uniqueness of the game/experience. The sound design is simple too, making it complementary to the world. The most unique part is of course, the "external" experience outside of the game; the folders being created, the text pages leading you through the puzzles, on your computer etc. People seem to give a lot of credit to [horror] games that interact with the user/play outside of the games window, such as breaking the 4th wall, reading your pc info, saying the name of the owner of the pc you are playing the steam game in, Doki Doki Literature club is probably the biggest one that comes to mind. And don't get me wrong, I think that's a creepy and cool feature that they should use from time to time! But as far as I know, this game was one of the first to try this intrusive feature that some don't give credit for, and furthermore, making it the core idea of the whole game; a creepy, stalking entity that's like a sentient computer virus that wants to befriend and play with you.

[spoiler]The finale/end of the game was SO freaky, I won't go into details but I haven't felt my hair raise from a game in many years. For a moment I was contemplating even relaunching the game and waiting until the morning after to continue playing in broad daylight instead. As of writing this review, apparently the end of IMSCARED isn't over either, and I'm glad I finally got to playing this game when theres news of a part 2(?)[/spoiler]

[h1]One of the best indie horror titles on Steam.[/h1]

You probably remember watching this game's early builds being played through by your favorite youtubers a good 10 years ago. You'd be surprised to see that after such long time the game's core style undoubtebly stays the same. At first glance, you can walk, look around, interact with the environment, and that's pretty much it. 
Zanotti, however, surprises the player throughout the whole game with sections that [b]break the 4th wall[/b] and require manipulation of game files, accessing URL links in your browser, or inputting secret codes in the game to progress it in secret ways, all in a very well implemented meta-gaming system. It is for sure one of the game's most interesting aspects

It's visual identity presents the player with extremely simple graphics that excell in being unnerving through creativity in the usage of color, lightning, darkness, fog, sprite silhouettes and textures.
The game pairs that with a sound identity that knows when to be subtle and when to be intense, creating a dense and deeply creepy atmosphere through a very effective combo. 
Zanotti's lo-fi sound and visual design is not only used for obtaining scary aesthetics, but also for gameplay purposes. It's not uncommon for there to be passages in the game where you guide yourself both through little details in the game's textures, but also through sound, while also being scared by both. The main ones coming to mind are the parking lot section and the gramophone maze section (with this last one being rather infamous for it's [b]RNG[/b], wich I understand).

Finally, the story, while interesting and touching, is notoriously difficult to understand. Not because of some level of complexity, but because it is very misteriously presented. 
Zanotti's intent is clearly to be misteryous, subtle, foggy, unclear in every aspect of the game's presentation. However that can generate some frustration in the player when they finish the game's multiple endings and are still left with a feeling of not knowing what any of it meant (because it clearly has some meaning). And after spending some time thinking about it, they will find that the story and messages are not [b]that[/b] deep. Fitting for an indie game, but not extraordinary.

In conclusion, IMSCARED is a [b]must have[/b] for horror and indie fans, especially for such a low price. While not being perfect, Zanotti's creation is lasting, engaging, creative, fun, and, most importantly, [b]very scary[/b].

[h2]Fourth wall breaking (trying to) [/h2]
IMSCARED gives very raw pixels, a haunting Whiteface, and tries to invade your desktop! There are several incoherent locations that you visit. 

You can question the originality of the scares, but as a whole I found the game memorable. There is one level, with the record player, that is truly abnoxious! It relies on stereo sound to ascertain the direction of the record player. The developer has a different idea about stereo than the average player, because I had no clue where it came from. The average jumpscare from the game is tolerable, in that level not! 

Now I have a personal vendetta with the game... At the very last level I messed up an achievement by making the wrong choice. And that resets the whole game... There is a way to edit the save config, but that doesn't seem to work. Now the game was fine for one playthrough, but I'm not really looking forward to a second one. That says it all I guess... This review will be in three parts, covering the 2012, 2016, and 2022 versions of IMSCARED. I've played all versions as they came out, with the 2016 version being the first thing I play after resetting my computer. I've played this game over ten times and gifted it to more than ten people. I love it and consider it one of the greatest horror games ever. If you want the short version: get this game now. It's unlike anything you will ever play. Even after all these years, no other game has executed what IMSCARED did. It was one of the first Steam games I got, and it holds a special place in my heart.

IMSCARED stands out in its sound design, art style, and gameplay even more than a decade later. The game breaks the fourth wall by creating files on your computer. This out of the box puzzle solving approach remains supreme in its execution and creativity. The game is so much more than just a horror game. It always felt to me like an emotional journey, with more to the story than just scares. It is not a mindless horror cliché.

One issue I have with the game is the lack of cloud saving. Every time I reset my computer, everything gets wiped, and I have to start again. This was fine before the 2022 version, but now there are files you need to keep to access future new content. Otherwise, you must start from scratch. This wasn't a big deal before since it's not a long game, and I already know all the solutions and where to go. However, with the 2022 version, you must download the test build and go through the entire scenario again. While not terrible, it is tedious. The thought of having to play through the game again just to reach the new content makes me less excited. I wish the cloud feature was enabled for this game.

[h1] [u] 2012 [/u] [/h1]
The 2012 version felt like a taste of what was to come. It was groundbreaking for its time and still is. It served as a demo of what’s to come, showcasing the game's unique mechanics and atmosphere.

[h1] [u] 2016 [/u] [/h1]
This version is where the game fully became realized, feeling like a fully fleshed-out game. The fourth wall-breaking puzzles were, and still are, mind-blowing to me. It felt like an unstable program in your computer. The ending feels so fitting and brings everything together.

[h1] [u] 2022 [/u] [/h1]
First, this version changed engines so other versions of the game can be ported to phones and other platforms. This introduced some drawbacks, such as tamer out of game puzzles and no window pop up asking, "what's my name." Instead, it uses in-game input, which slightly changes some of the game's appeal but not by much. This was done to avoid your computer thinking the game is trying to modify it. However, aside from these changes, it is essentially the 2016 version.

The 2022 version also adds extra content after you finish the game. Just when I thought the game couldn't get more creative, it did. It asks you to return to one of the levels, download a test build from Itch.io, play it to get some specific files, merge them with the 2022 version file, and then enter new content that will change with every major update of the game. How crazy is that! The game feels alive even after all these years. It’s a game that came out in 2012 and is still being updated to perfection to this day.

I am looking forward to what’s to come. I love this game and highly recommend everyone to play it. Horror fans and non-horror fans alike. There's more to come, so join in or you'll miss out.

IMSCARED, developed and published by Ivan Zanotti’s MyMadnessWorks, is an unsettling and inventive indie horror game that dismantles the boundary between player and machine. Rather than relying on traditional scares or realistic visuals, it constructs its terror through psychological manipulation and meta-horror design. From the moment it begins, the game warns you that it will attempt to deceive and disturb you beyond its own interface—a promise it delivers with unnerving precision. What follows is not a typical survival horror experience, but a haunting experiment in immersion where the game itself seems alive, aware, and intent on making you question what’s real.

The experience begins in an intentionally primitive-looking 3D space—a dimly lit room rendered in low-resolution textures reminiscent of early 1990s PC titles. You awaken with no clear instructions, only a locked door and a cryptic message hinting at something you must find: a “heart.” As you explore, you soon encounter “White Face,” a ghostly entity that stalks you through shifting corridors and repeating rooms. It’s not the kind of monster that lunges from shadows for a quick shock; instead, it observes, toys with you, and manifests through the game’s glitches and distortions. The further you progress, the more the world collapses into surreal loops, with rooms reshaping themselves and messages breaking the fourth wall. You realize that IMSCARED is not just presenting horror—it’s performing it directly through your computer, by creating files, altering directories, and simulating crashes to amplify your unease.

This manipulation of the player’s environment is where IMSCARED becomes truly disturbing. It will close itself unexpectedly, generate cryptic text documents on your desktop, or even mimic system errors. These tricks aren’t gimmicks but integral parts of the narrative, forming a dialogue between player and program. The game uses these external interactions to make you complicit in its horror—you aren’t simply playing a haunted game, you’re participating in its haunting. The sense of intrusion is what makes IMSCARED so effective. At one moment you may be searching a room for a key, and the next, you’re checking your actual computer folders to decipher a hidden message. The fear it evokes is personal, as though something inside your machine is watching you back.

Visually, the game’s crude presentation works in its favor. The blocky environments and flat textures evoke a bygone era of gaming, recalling early horror experiments that relied on atmosphere rather than fidelity. The simplicity strips away comfort, leaving space for the imagination to fill in the blanks. Every corridor feels wrong, every sound slightly too distorted to trust. The audio design heightens this discomfort—mechanical drones, abrupt silences, and looping static create an oppressive sense of isolation. Even the game’s music, sparse and low in fidelity, feels corrupted, as if the data itself is decaying. The minimalism of the visuals and sound becomes part of the storytelling, reflecting the idea that fear is not in what you see, but what you perceive.

Gameplay itself revolves around exploration and puzzle-solving, but these mechanics are subservient to atmosphere. You collect items, unlock doors, and uncover fragments of story, yet the focus is never on achieving mastery—it’s on enduring the dread of uncertainty. The puzzles are deliberately cryptic, often requiring you to step outside the game window to find clues or re-launch the application to access new sequences. Some players may find this frustrating, as progress can depend on non-traditional logic and an understanding of how the game manipulates its own structure. However, this unpredictability is part of the experience. The act of restarting, of watching the game seemingly rewrite its rules, becomes a ritual of dread. Every relaunch feels like returning to a place you were never meant to revisit.

What makes IMSCARED so memorable is how it weaponizes its limitations. There are no elaborate cutscenes, no cinematic monsters, and no hand-holding narrative. Its horror exists in suggestion and implication—its glitches, its files, its false exits. The illusion of control is constantly stripped away until you begin to feel less like a player and more like a victim of the software itself. It’s a deeply self-aware piece of interactive art that examines the relationship between creator and audience, using the language of games—crashes, saves, directories, achievements—as its storytelling tools. Each scare is earned through psychological tension rather than cheap spectacle, and the result is a kind of existential dread that lingers long after the program is closed.

IMSCARED is not a game for everyone. Its abstract storytelling, lack of visual polish, and unconventional mechanics can alienate players expecting traditional horror or straightforward objectives. Yet for those who embrace its experimental nature, it offers an experience unlike any other—a work that transforms the act of playing into an act of vulnerability. It doesn’t just break the fourth wall; it erases it entirely, making you feel complicit in its haunting. Few games so effectively capture the feeling of being alone in front of a computer screen at night, wondering if what you’re seeing might somehow be seeing you too. In its raw simplicity and unnerving ingenuity, IMSCARED achieves what few horror titles dare to attempt: it makes fear intimate, personal, and disturbingly real.

At least it's cheap. IMSCARED is a meta-horror game where the experience involves your entire computer system, and not just the application itself. It's a bit difficult to start up its tools, as it relies on having a desktop folder to place information for the puzzles into, but the rest of its creepy effects on your computer seem to work reliably. It seems alright at first, and kind of reminds me of the atmosphere of games like Ghoul's Forest, due to the ominous darkness in the game, but I don't think it provides a satisfying or believable setting in its visual design. The graphics aren't just bad, they're terribly done, to the point that it's really hard to read things, or to even figure out what some of the things your looking at even are. If it was a "real" game, even as an experiment, it's likely that someone would have put more work into its visuals, as even old computer games never looked this bad. 

[h1] What I Enjoyed [/h1]
[list]
[*][b]IMSCARED is sometimes frightening[/b]. Before you're aware of what's going on, and when you're entering into new challenges, the atmosphere is sufficiently effective and the scares are shocking, even if you can anticipate when they will appear. It may look like garbage a lot of the time, but the startle from seeing some of its monsters lunge at you was able to scare me several times. Unfortunately, the narrative, locations, and general events of the game are not particularly scary or inventive for a horror genre. The crashing built into the game to convince you that it's "glitched" or "broken" isn't frightening at all, and is so heavy-handed and common it becomes irritating.
[*]The puzzles are often good. There's a few real doozies hidden in this game, and the mechanics of how it works with its computer folder, text documents, and the like can be really fun. Unfortunately, the game is largely a collectathon built around keys, and it can be mystifying what one is expected to do, or where to go--even with the hints provided by the game files. 
[*]The sound quality is fitting for the visual and gameplay direction. The sounds the monsters make, as well as the tone of footsteps, items, and the like is immersive. 
[/list]

[h1]What I Disliked[/h1]
[list]
[*][b]The gameplay is awful[/b]! There was never an old game that controlled like this one does, with full movement in any direction and quick spinning of where you are facing. As a result, this is one of the main things that makes the game feel so fake. It's obvious it was made in 2012 and not in the 80s or 90s, and couldn't possibly be haunted or broken, but was designed that way. As I said, the game is just built on collecting objects, and there's basically nothing to do but press E at relevant points, and crouch just so you can pick stuff up. The rest of the game is a walking simulator where you constantly have to restart because it does a fake-crash every thirty seconds anytime something scary happens. It's like a story that doesn't know how to continue after it has reached the climax, and I don't know if it's worse that the game keeps doing the same crash over and over, or if it would just reset me to a checkpoint. I'm leaning to the crashing, since it takes more time and is so unimaginative you begin to just expect it. Worst of all, you have to collect all of the achievements to complete the game, which essentially requires using a walkthrough, even if it gives you shortcuts for getting close to the ending. 
[*]The atmosphere of having a "game" with the entire computer and not just the application is executed poorly. I enjoy it when a puzzle requires you to do pseudo-programming by changing values in the text boxes, or take hints from files, but the youtube videos that play are awful, annoying, and fake. The programmer's voice is obnoxious, and his idea of scary is childish. And I can't get over how annoying it that it wants to pretend to crash constantly. It was cool when Undertale or Doki Doki Literature Club tried this, as it was done with subtlety and some sense of taste, rather than being something the creator had to rely on because there was NOTHING else interesting or appealing about his video game. 
[*]The story is bad. It's a boring plot that makes no sense and asks for arbitrary emotional reactions that would not coincide with its themes, and its written badly. Perhaps it's the translation, but if the developer knows English, he should have been able to find something satisfying in the localization. It doesn't have to be the Divine Comedy, but the game honestly feels like it was written by a person with one digit IQ. 
[*]It's full of boring segments like a hedgemaze or a freezer that just serve to artifically lengthen a game that's likely too short to even be released. The gameplay puzzles in these sections also don't work well, and between the headache from puzzling about abstract ways to continue, from having to stare at the awful graphics and listen to the grating sounds, it's hard to find any reason to even continue.
[/list]

IAMSCARED is not like other games. It’s “meta” and it’s spooky. I can see how the designer was aiming to create a unique experience, and I commend him for this, but in the end I think he was only partially successful in the execution of his goal and in creating a game I wanted to play. I ended up just watching my friend play through most of it and if it was only me I would have given up before I finished. 
My thoughts (very mild spoilers ahead):

* The meta-puzzles (puzzles which require you to look outside the game itself) are clever and out of the ordinary.  

* The more traditional puzzles are all pretty simple. The answer is usually obvious although sometimes you might have a hard time because of the game controls or because you can’t find something. 

* For the most part the game succeeds in creating an eerie atmosphere. The sound, the way the environment looks, the creepy messages and enigmatic characters….

* As others have pointed out, part of the scare factor is a result of your annoyingly small field of vision. You can only see like five feet in front of you so it’s easy to run into something surprising. 

* Related to the limited field of vision, the game has a lot of jump scares. These are fun at first but get old fast, especially if you are caught by the monster and have to replay the same part again and again. This is frustrating; but more than that it can destroy the scare factor.

* The controls! You need to use the WASD keys to move around (this alone is almost a deal breaker for me) and the game is not very responsive, so your movements are jerky. It’s also easy to get stuck in a corner or at the edge of a wall (this is  just a result of poor game design/programming). It’s particularly frustrating in parts where you’re being chased and need to run.

*The graphics and the environment: I have mixed feelings. I see what the designer was going for with very basic, very retro graphics. The game’s look reminded me of EGA computer games and also the LSD: Dream Emulator on Playstation. So this gives the game a dream/nightmare vibe and it fits well with the “deconstructing the game” aspect of IAMSCARED. On the other hand, this really goes beyond artfully pixelated and sometimes just feels insufficiently detailed (get close enough to something and you’ll see it’s just colored blocks). 

* More than the graphics, I disliked the low level of interactivity. 90% of the objects you see (bookcases, cabinets, tables, shopping carts) are just decoration you can do nothing with. You’ll spend a lot of the game going up to things and trying to interact with them only to find out “nope.”

*Related to the simple puzzles and the static non-interactive environment, there are a lot of times when it seemed like I reached a dead-end and needed to do something (like find a key or a secret passage or something) but the answer was that I needed to trigger something like a “cut scene” and then when I came back the way would be clear.

*The story: again mixed feelings. In the game you’ll encounter one or two important characters. You’re given vague hints as to what their story is, but it’s left pretty fuzzy. On one hand, this is good because you need to fill in the blanks yourself and it’s open to interpretation. On the other hand, maybe there’s just not enough there.

*That leads into my final gripe which is that there’s no pay off. Towards the very end, the game throws up such a barrier it’s almost like the designer doesn’t want you to finish the game. And the ending(s?) are kind of anti-climactic; it made me question whether it was even worth it.  

TL;DR: All-in-all, if I put aside the annoying controls, I’d say I got something out of IAMSCARED and enjoyed the unique meta-puzzles but so many things frustrated or bored me that I would never have finished the game on my own.

Some parts of the game rely on sound within a 3D soundscape, and sound seems to originate in one position but does not change relative to your movement. Certain actions like climbing a ladder or printing tickets have a gratingly loud volume for no reason. 

Many achievements were very arbitrary, and ended up being necessary to finish the game. This review contains spoilers.

I tried really hard to like IMSCARED. A game that has the player interacting with an entity that communicates with them by creating text files on the player's desktop is intriguing. The visual style, while not entirely original, feels dated, a commonly overlooked way to create unease with the player. The game's price point is also low and suitable for a game with this level of content. However, IMSCARED stumbles in a lot of areas and left me frustrated with it. I'll break down what I didn't like about the game.

1. I said in my introductory paragraph that I found the interaction between the player and the game to be intriguing. While it is, it's also a bit awkwardly implemented. There are several points in the game where you need to be reading a text file while playing the game. During these segments, you can put the game in windowed mode, but the window is incredibly tiny and the controls sometimes glitch out while you're trying to go back and forth between the text file and game.

2. The game "crashes" and closes itself on several occasions. This harkens back to Eternal Darkness: Sanity's Requiem and the original Metal Gear Solid, where the game attempts to fool the player into thinking that the game is actually interacting with something in the real world. I initially didn't mind this, but the game began to abuse it. If you get caught by the monster at certain points in the game, the game will close and you'll be brought back to your desktop. There were points where you're required to solve puzzles with little to no conveyance as the monster chases you around the environment. If you get caught, you're brought back to your desktop, losing your progress up until the start of the puzzle. I actually took breaks from this fairly short game because I was so frustrated with my constant failures. I also imagine my Steam friends were getting annoyed, constantly seeing me start and stop playing the game. If the game maybe brought you back to the menu screen when you died rather than completely closing out, this wouldn't be so much of an issue.

3. Jump scares, jump scares, jump scares. I see a lot of reviews praising this game for being "truly scary", but I see very little criticism of its over-reliance on jump scares. While I'll admit that the game made me feel uneasy at times with its retro atmosphere and creepy ambience, there were way more occasions where something would pop out and make a loud noise at me for a cheap scare. There are points where an overlay will flash on the screen with a loud noise and the game will close, something entirely jumpy and even more forgettable. The worst offender, however, is a puzzle about 3/4 of the way through the game where the player is tasked with finding record players in a maze and destroying them. You're being chased by the monster during this segment, but weird figures will come down from the ceiling and screech at you for absolutely no reason. They add nothing to the experience at all and don't play into the puzzle in any way, just being added as cheap scares to make the situation less scary than it would have been if you were simply being chased.

4. The game is somewhat fragmented. There isn't really a hub location until the very end of the game, and the areas you're going through have little to nothing to do with one another. You go to a supermarket, a train station, a basement area and a hedgemaze throughout the course of the game. These areas aren't really connected to each other until the very end, and even then the game only connects them through a series of doors that teleport you to them. Some of the areas even require you to input different things into a text prompt, something that is vital near the end of the game if you didn't get all of the achievements (I'll expand on this later). Overall, you find yourself teleporting from area to area. The game will close, and you'll find yourself in an entirely new location without any explanation as to why. As a result, nothing feels familiar and the game feels stitched together, like a collection of different ideas.

5. Movement is awkard and actually somewhat buggy. It's fairly simple, being mapped to the WASD keys for moving, the Shift key for sprinting, and the Ctrl key for crouching. However, it's easy to get "caught" on objects, requiring you to reposition the camera in order to move again. If you want to try this, you simply need to walk along a wall and rotate the camera towards it. You'll eventually get stuck and won't be able to move unless you rotate the camera away from the wall. This wouldn't be so bad if there weren't actual segments where you need to get through cramped spaces and you're constantly getting stuck on both sides of the wall. There's also a segment where you're being chased through a hallway, and while I only got caught on a bookshelf once, it still exemplified how buggy the movement is. It's also worth noting that if you crouch next to certain objects, you can clip through them, which looks very awkward and allows you to peer inside some things.

6. Near the end of the game, the player is about to go through the last door when the game prompts them that they need to get all of the achievements in order to proceed. At first I thought this was a trick, but it's serious. Closing the game will bring you back to the start of the game, which has opened up some new doors to previous parts of the game where you can obtain these achievements. When I started this game, it was less than a week old. The achievement list gives absolutely no clues as to how the achievements are obtained and the discussion board was barren of help. This left me stumbling about, trying to figure out how to get the last few achievements so that I could actually finish the game. Some of these achievements are incredibly obscure, requiring you to do things like knock on a wall and set your system clock to certain times in order to get some items. Achievements are meant to entertain completionists, not frustrate people who just want to experience the game.

I truly, dearly wanted to enjoy IMSCARED. It does some really interesting things and has a very low price point. However, the times where I was wowed were undermined by the amount of times I was frustrated or disappointed. In the end, this is just a short indie horror game with lots of jump scares and a somewhat entertaining fourth-wall mechanic. It's not incredibly noteworthy and I can think of other games that do fourth-wall breaking better with less frustrations and more polish.
